definition:
Israel is the people God chose from among the nations to be his own, the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, through whom he promised to bless “all the families of the earth” (Genesis 12:3). The doctrine of Israel in God's purpose asks what that choice was for, what became of it when Israel failed and was scattered, and what it means after the coming of Jesus, who was himself an Israelite and Israel's Messiah. Scripture holds together two truths that Christians have often found hard to hold at once. Israel's calling is for the sake of the world, so the promise reaches the Gentiles through Abraham's family. And God's calling of Israel stands: Paul writes that “God's gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). Christians agree on both and differ on how the church and the Jewish people now relate and what the promises to Israel mean for the future. (The study on election treats God's choosing more broadly, and the site's page on covenant frameworks compares the systems built on these questions.)

The name Israel first belongs to a man. After Jacob wrestles through the night, he is told, “Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed” (Genesis 32:28). Grammatically the name has God (El) as its subject, and scholars propose meanings such as ‘God strives’ or ‘God rules’; Genesis explains it by a play on the verb for struggling, and that story, not the name's etymology, carries its meaning. The name passes to Jacob's twelve sons and their tribes, ‘the sons of Israel’, then to the nation, then to the northern kingdom after the division, and finally to the whole people again. It occurs about 2,500 times in the Old Testament. The earliest mention outside the Bible is on the stele of the Egyptian king Merneptah (about 1208 BC). Hebrew calls Israel God's ‘am, ‘people’, a word of kinship, more often than a goy, ‘nation’, and speaks of the qahal, the ‘assembly’ gathered before God, which the Septuagint often translates ekklēsia, the word the New Testament uses for the church. In the New Testament Israēl appears about seventy times, beside Ioudaios, ‘Jew’ (originally ‘Judean’).
ot:
Israel's story begins in the promise to Abraham: a great nation, a land, and blessing for the world (Genesis 12:1-3). Genesis follows the promise through Isaac and Jacob to the twelve tribes, “twelve in all” (Genesis 49:28), and the number twelve remains the sign of the whole people for the rest of Scripture, from the twelve pillars at Sinai (Exodus 24:4) to Elijah's twelve stones (1 Kings 18:31). In Egypt God calls Israel “My firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22), a title of love and inheritance. At Sinai he makes them his “treasured possession out of all the nations” and “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:5-6): a people set between God and the world to show what he is like. Deuteronomy insists the choice rests on nothing in Israel. They were “the fewest of all peoples” and were chosen “because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers” (Deuteronomy 7:7-8).

The histories show how hard the calling was to live. Israel became a kingdom under Saul, David, and Solomon, and after Solomon's death, about 930 BC, the ten northern tribes broke away with the cry, “To your tents, O Israel” (1 Kings 12:16). From then on ‘Israel’ usually means the northern kingdom and ‘Judah’ the southern. The north fell to Assyria in 722 BC and its people were deported, and Judah went into exile in Babylon after Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC (see the study on exile). The prophets interpret all this as the covenant's judgment. Election is not a shield: “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2). Amos even asks whether Israel is any different from the Cushites before God (Amos 9:7). Hosea names his son Lo-ammi, “for you are not My people” (Hosea 1:9), and in the next breath promises that “in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God’” (1:10).

Two ideas grow out of judgment. The first is the remnant. Isaiah foresees that “only a remnant will return” (Isaiah 10:22), a faithful core through whom God keeps his promise. The second is a restored and reunited Israel. Ezekiel joins two sticks, Judah and Joseph, into one, and hears God promise, “I will make them one nation in the land” under one king (Ezekiel 37:17, 22). Jeremiah ties the continuance of Israel to the fixed order of sun and moon (Jeremiah 31:35-37), and pairs it with the new covenant made “with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” (31:31).

Isaiah's servant songs press further. God calls Israel “My servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen” (Isaiah 41:8), and appoints his servant “to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations” (42:6). In Isaiah 49 the servant is named Israel (49:3), yet he is sent “to bring Jacob back to Him” (49:5), and God says, “It is not enough for You to be My Servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob”, and adds, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (49:6). Jewish interpreters have usually read the servant as the people of Israel or its faithful remnant; the New Testament identifies him with Jesus. Both readings notice something true in the text: the servant is Israel, and he is also one who restores Israel. The Old Testament closes with the people back in the land, the temple rebuilt, and the promises of a united, renewed Israel that blesses the nations still waiting.
nt:
The New Testament opens inside Israel's hope. Mary sings that God “has helped His servant Israel” (Luke 1:54), Simeon calls the child “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel” (Luke 2:32), and the disciples on the Emmaus road say, “we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). Matthew tells Jesus' story as Israel's story lived again: he is called out of Egypt, applying Hosea's words about Israel, “Out of Egypt I called My Son” (Matthew 2:15; Hosea 11:1), and he is tested forty days in the wilderness, answering with Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:1-11). Jesus says, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1), taking up the Old Testament picture of Israel as God's vine (Psalm 80:8; Isaiah 5:7). He chose twelve apostles, and the number spoke: they will sit on thrones “judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30). His mission was first “to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24), yet he promised that many would come from east and west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matthew 8:11). He grieved over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37-39), and in the parable of the tenants he warned the temple leaders that “the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit” (Matthew 21:43). Interpreters differ on whether that saying concerns Jerusalem's leadership, the nation, or both.

In Acts the gospel goes first to Israel. Peter calls “all Israel” to know that God has made Jesus Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36), and tells the crowd they are “sons of the prophets and of the covenant” (3:25). Thousands of Jews believe, and the church is at first entirely Jewish. The disciples ask whether Jesus will now “restore the kingdom to Israel” (1:6), and he does not deny the hope but directs them to the witness of the Spirit to the ends of the earth. As Gentiles come in, Paul applies Isaiah's servant text to his mission (13:47, quoting Isaiah 49:6), and to the end he insists he is on trial “because of the hope of Israel” (28:20; compare 26:6-7).

Paul's letters hold the tension most openly. Gentile believers, once “alienated from the commonwealth of Israel” (Ephesians 2:12), are now “fellow citizens with the saints” (2:19), for Christ has “made the two one” and created “one new man out of the two” (2:14-15). In Galatians 3:29 those who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed. Paul can say “it is we who are the circumcision” (Philippians 3:3) and bless “the Israel of God” (Galatians 6:16), a phrase some read as the church of Jews and Gentiles and others as Jewish believers or Israel as a whole. Yet in Romans 9 to 11 he refuses to let Israel's story be over. He grieves for his people, to whom belong “the adoption as sons; theirs the divine glory and the covenants; theirs the giving of the law, the temple worship, and the promises”, and from whom comes the Messiah (Romans 9:4-5). He answers that “It is not as though God's word has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel” (9:6), and that even now there is a remnant chosen by grace (11:5). He asks, “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (11:1), and pictures one olive tree from which some natural branches were broken off and into which Gentile branches were grafted, warning Gentiles, “do not boast over those branches” (11:18). He expects the natural branches to be grafted back in (11:23-24) and concludes that “A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved” (11:25-26). Regarding election, Paul writes, “they are loved on account of the patriarchs” (11:28).

Other writers use Israel's titles for the church. Peter tells scattered believers, “you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession” (1 Peter 2:9), words drawn from Exodus 19, and applies Hosea's promise to them (2:10). James writes “To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion” (James 1:1). Revelation hears the number of the sealed “from all the tribes of Israel” (Revelation 7:4) and then sees “a multitude too large to count, from every nation” (7:9), and the new Jerusalem bears on its gates the names of the twelve tribes and on its foundations the names of the twelve apostles (21:12-14). Whatever else these texts mean, the Bible ends with Israel and the nations in one city.

keyTexts.why: The promise to Abraham: a great nation, and through it blessing for all the families of the earth. Israel's calling is for the world from the start.
Jacob wrestles through the night and receives the name Israel. The people's name begins in struggle with God and blessing from him.
Israel is made God's treasured possession, a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation, a people set between God and the nations.
God chose Israel not for its size or merit but because he loved them and kept his oath to their fathers.
The servant, named Israel, is sent to restore Israel and to be a light to the nations. Acts applies the passage to Paul's mission.
The new covenant is promised to the house of Israel and Judah, and Israel's continuance is tied to the fixed order of creation.
The two sticks joined into one: God promises a reunited Israel under one king, cleansed and dwelling with him.
Judgment names Israel ‘not My people’, and mercy promises they will be called children of the living God. Paul and Peter both use it.
Jesus promises the Twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel in the renewal of all things.
Paul on trial for the hope of the promise that Israel's twelve tribes hope to attain, which he locates in the resurrection.
Israel's privileges listed, the Messiah among them, and Paul's claim that God's word has not failed, since not all who are descended from Israel are Israel.
God has not rejected his people. The olive tree, the hardening in part, and the promise that all Israel will be saved, the center of every Christian debate on Israel.
Gentiles once alienated from the commonwealth of Israel are made fellow citizens, one new man in Christ with Jewish believers.
Israel's titles from Exodus 19 and Hosea's promise are applied to believers in Christ.
The new Jerusalem bears the names of the twelve tribes on its gates and of the twelve apostles on its foundations.

history:
The earliest church was Jewish, and its first great argument, settled at Jerusalem about AD 49 (Acts 15), was whether Gentiles could belong without becoming Jews. Within a century the church was mostly Gentile, and its writers began to claim Israel's name for themselves. Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho (about 155 to 160) called Christians the true spiritual Israel. Melito of Sardis, in his Easter homily On the Pascha (about 160 to 180), accused Israel of murdering God, a charge that echoed for centuries. Augustine offered a different theory: in the City of God (18.46, about 425), reading Psalm 59:11, he taught that the Jews were dispersed but preserved as witnesses, carrying the Scriptures that testify to Christ, and should not be destroyed. That teaching protected Jews in some ways while fixing them in a subordinate place. In practice Christian Europe often treated Jews with contempt and violence. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) required Jews to wear distinctive dress, and Jews were expelled from England in 1290 and from Spain in 1492. Martin Luther wrote That Jesus Christ Was Born a Jew (1523), hoping for Jewish conversion, and twenty years later On the Jews and Their Lies (1543), which urged burning synagogues. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America formally repudiated those writings in 1994.

Readings of Romans 11 divided early. Calvin took ‘all Israel’ to mean the whole people of God, Jews and Gentiles together. Many Puritans and Reformed divines expected a future large-scale conversion of the Jewish people, and the Westminster Larger Catechism (1647, question 191) teaches believers to pray, as part of the coming of God's kingdom, that the Jews would be called. In the nineteenth century John Nelson Darby taught that Israel and the church are distinct peoples with distinct destinies, and through the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) that view shaped much of American evangelicalism, including support for a Jewish return to the land. The Balfour Declaration (1917) and the founding of the State of Israel in 1948 made these questions political as well as theological.

The Holocaust forced a reckoning. Karl Barth, writing Church Dogmatics II/2 (1942) as the Nazi state persecuted the Jews, taught that Israel and the church together form the one community elected in Jesus Christ, so that the church cannot call itself elect and Israel rejected. The Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965, section 4) repudiated the charge that the Jews as a people were guilty of Christ's death, cited Romans 11:28-29, and deplored antisemitism. Since then many churches have issued similar statements, and a body of theology has named and criticized supersessionism, the view that the church has replaced Israel in God's purpose. R. Kendall Soulen's The God of Israel and Christian Theology (1996) distinguished its forms, and Messianic Jewish theologians such as Mark Kinzer (Postmissionary Messianic Judaism, 2005) argue that Jewish believers in Jesus should remain a distinct Torah-observant community within the one body. At the same time, Reformed writers such as John Murray (commentary on Romans, 1959 and 1965) defended a future conversion of Israel within the one church, and others, such as O. Palmer Robertson (The Israel of God, 2000), read Romans 11 as the ongoing ingathering of Jewish believers across this age. The site's page on covenant frameworks sets out how the major systems answer.

differ.view: Fulfillment: the church as Israel renewed in the Messiah
differ.body: Israel's calling was always to be the people through whom God would bless the world, and Jesus, the faithful Israelite, fulfills that calling. Those who belong to him, Jew and Gentile, are Abraham's seed (Galatians 3:29), the circumcision (Philippians 3:3), and the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16); Peter gives them Israel's titles (1 Peter 2:9). On this view ‘all Israel’ in Romans 11:26 is the whole people of God, gathered from Jews and Gentiles by the time the full number has come in, and the promises of land and temple are fulfilled in Christ and the new creation. Calvin read Romans 11 this way, and N. T. Wright argues a version of it. Defenders stress that this is not replacement: Gentiles are grafted into Israel's own tree, and Jews are welcome back into it.

differ.view: One people, with a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ
differ.body: There is one olive tree and one people of God in Christ, so Israel has no way to God apart from its Messiah. But Paul distinguishes ‘Israel’ from the Gentiles throughout Romans 11, and ‘all Israel’ in 11:26 means the Jewish people as a whole, who will turn to Christ in large numbers when the full number of the Gentiles has come in. Their acceptance will be “life from the dead” (Romans 11:15). This was the hope of many Puritans, is reflected in the Westminster Larger Catechism's prayer for the calling of the Jews, and was defended by Charles Hodge and John Murray. It expects no separate national program, only the natural branches grafted back into their own tree.

differ.view: The elect remnant gathered through the age
differ.body: Romans 9 to 11 answers the question whether God's word has failed, and Paul's answer is the remnant: not all who are descended from Israel are Israel (9:6), and at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace (11:5). ‘All Israel’ is the sum of elect Jews saved throughout history, grafted back in one by one as they believe, alongside the full number of the Gentiles. The ‘and so’ of 11:26 describes the manner of Israel's salvation, not a later sequence. William Hendriksen and O. Palmer Robertson hold forms of this view, which keeps a real place for Jewish people in God's purpose without predicting a single future event.

differ.view: Distinction: Israel and the church as distinct peoples (dispensational)
differ.body: God made unconditional promises to Israel as a nation, including the land and a Davidic throne, and the prophets expect a restored nation in the land (Ezekiel 37). These promises must be fulfilled to the people who received them, or God's word would fail. The church, born at Pentecost, shares the spiritual blessings of the new covenant but does not take Israel's place, which is why Paul still speaks of Israel after the church exists. Romans 11:26 foretells a national turning of Israel at Christ's return, followed by the fulfillment of the national promises in his kingdom. Darby, Scofield, and Ryrie taught the view in classic form; progressive dispensationalists such as Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock stress greater unity while still expecting a future for national Israel.

God's covenant with the Jewish people is irrevocable (Romans 11:29), and the New Testament church was a community of Jews and Gentiles in which Jewish believers remained Jews and kept the law (Acts 21:20). The church is not a replacement for Israel but an extension of Israel's blessing to the nations, and the distinction between Jew and Gentile in Christ is a gift to be kept, not erased. Christian theology should therefore reckon with the Jewish people's ongoing covenant identity and, for Jewish believers, with Torah observance as covenant faithfulness. R. Kendall Soulen and Mark Kinzer represent this approach. Its advocates differ among themselves on how the Jewish people's ongoing covenant relates to faith in Jesus, while agreeing that he is Israel's Messiah.

errors:
The church has come, often far too slowly, to reject the teaching that God has cast off the Jewish people, that his covenant with them is revoked, or that Jews as a people bear guilt for Christ's death. Paul's own words forbid it: “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1), and Gentile believers are warned not to boast over the natural branches (11:18). That error, and the contempt it fed, prepared the ground for centuries of expulsions and massacres and was exploited in the Holocaust. It also misreads the Gospels, which present Jesus' death as the act of Jewish and Roman leaders together and as the will of God for the salvation of all, including those who crucified him. None of the positions set out above teaches it.

The church has also rejected the opposite errors. Marcion cut Christ loose from Israel and its Scriptures, but the Messiah is “from them” (Romans 9:5), and “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22). Another error treats Israel's election as a guarantee of favor apart from faithfulness, which the prophets and John the Baptist rejected (Amos 3:2; Matthew 3:9). And most confessing churches have declined the proposal that Jews are saved through the Sinai covenant apart from Jesus, since the apostles preached him as Israel's own Messiah, “first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). A last distortion reads current politics directly into prophecy, whether to baptize every act of a modern state or to deny it any legitimacy. Christians who differ on the promises can still agree that the Bible does not license either.
life:
For a Gentile Christian this doctrine is a lesson in humility and gratitude. Paul tells Gentile believers that they do not support the root, “but the root supports you” (Romans 11:18). Their faith rests on Israel's Scriptures, Israel's patriarchs, Israel's covenants, and Israel's Messiah, and the psalms they pray are Israel's prayers. To read the Old Testament as family history is to learn that faith has a long memory. It also calls Christians to repent of contempt for Jewish people wherever it survives, in speech, in preaching, or in careless readings of the Gospels, and to love Jewish neighbors as neighbors.

The doctrine also steadies hope. Israel's story shows God keeping his word through failure, judgment, scattering, and centuries of waiting; he disciplines his people but does not abandon them. Paul ends his hardest argument not with a system but with praise for the depth of God's riches and wisdom (Romans 11:33-36). Believers who disagree about Romans 11 can still share that praise, pray for the peace of Jerusalem, and look for the day when the city of God bears the names of Israel's tribes and the Lamb's apostles together.
questions: God chose Israel to be a blessing to all the families of the earth. How does knowing what Israel was chosen for change the way you read the Old Testament?
In Romans 11 Paul warns Gentile believers not to boast over the natural branches. What would that warning look like in the life of a church today?
The positions in this study read ‘all Israel will be saved’ in different ways. Which texts does each one lean on most, and what question would you want to ask each of them?
